provenance.method: Question created to expose a genuine catalogue gap. Current game pages contain some sensory and accessibility information, but the evidence is not consistent enough to rank games by sensory demand without overclaiming.

question: Which games have lower or more controllable sensory demands?
why_it_matters: Motion, flashes, colour, sound layering, camera movement and visual clutter can determine whether a game is usable even when its pace and failure structure are gentle.
current_understanding: The current catalogue is still not strong enough to rank games as low-sensory. Steam now exposes useful developer-declared accessibility features such as camera comfort and custom volume controls, which improves pre-purchase inspection, but declarations are not independent audits and coverage is incomplete across older titles. Minecraft has governed accessibility-setting context, while Tiny Glade and Cloud Gardens have documented low-objective creative structures but still include animated visual and sound environments. ND Oracle should not convert aesthetic words such as 'cozy' or 'soothing' into a sensory-accessibility score.
evidence_needed: Per-game first-party or specialist accessibility inventories covering motion, flashes, camera shake, field of view, audio channels, volume controls, colour/contrast, visual clutter and reduced-effects options, with platform/version provenance.
reopening_conditions: A sufficiently broad set of current accessibility records supports a bounded comparison.
A machine-readable game-facet model is adopted with explicit source provenance.
dissent: Sensory demand is highly individual and mode/platform dependent; a single global 'sensory intensity' rating would risk false precision.
